title: Nearly 90 US Politicians Pledge to Reject RSS-Linked Donations After Bhagwat's Madison Square Garden Rally
excerpt: The bipartisan pledge, led by Hindus for Human Rights Action and SACRED Acts, has sparked backlash from Hindu American groups who call it discriminatory profiling.
body:
• About 90 federal, state, and local politicians — including Reps. Ro Khanna and Pramila Jayapal — signed a six-page pledge to refuse campaign donations linked to the RSS
  • Rep. Ro Khanna donated away a $6,600 contribution he identified as tied to an alleged RSS-linked donor
  • The pledge follows RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat's August 29 rally at Madison Square Garden, attended by about 5,000 people from 250 Hindu American organizations
  • Hindu American groups including HAPAC, HAF, and Americans4Hindus condemned the campaign as religious profiling that could stigmatize ordinary Hindu American donors

About 90 U.S. politicians across eight states have signed a pledge to reject campaign donations from individuals and organizations linked to India's Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, the Hindu nationalist organization whose chief addressed thousands at Madison Square Garden last month.

The six-page pledge, announced on August 31 by Hindus for Human Rights Action and the South Asian American Coalition to Renew Democracy Acts (SACRED Acts), asks signatories to refuse future RSS-linked contributions and to return or redirect previously received funds to organizations "supporting democracy."

Who Signed the Pledge

The list includes prominent Indian-American lawmakers. Rep. Ro Khanna (D-CA) said he donated away a $6,600 contribution he identified as tied to an alleged RSS-linked donor. Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-WA), Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, and his former opponent Rep. Haley Stevens are also among the signatories.

https://x.com/RanaAyyub/status/2096985934659252501

The pledge covers politicians at every level — federal, state, and local — from both the Democratic and Republican parties, though most signatories are Democrats. Politicians and candidates across eight U.S. states have committed to the initiative, according to the organizing groups.

Bhagwat's Madison Square Garden Rally

The political move comes days after RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat addressed about 5,000 Hindu Americans at Madison Square Garden on August 29 at an event called the "Universal Oneness Celebration," organized by American Hindus for Engagement and Dialogue (AHEAD) Forum. About 250 Hindu American organizations participated.

"If any Hindu thinks that there should be no Muslim in Bharat, he will not remain Hindu. If you call yourself Hindu, you must believe all paths are leading to the same goal."

— Mohan Bhagwat, RSS chief, at Madison Square Garden

The rally drew large protests outside the venue. An interfaith coalition including Hindus for Human Rights, the Indian American Muslim Council, and the Interfaith Center of New York held a press conference at New York City Hall before the event, calling for its cancellation.

NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani, the city's first Indian-American mayor, publicly opposed the event, describing the RSS ideology as "exclusionary." He said, however, that he was unsure whether the city had jurisdiction to cancel a privately organized gathering.

The U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF) had separately urged the U.S. government to consider sanctions against RSS members, describing the organization as an "umbrella organization whose sub-groups have perpetrated attacks on religious minorities, including Christians and Muslims."

Hindu American Groups Push Back

The pledge has drawn sharp criticism from several Hindu American organizations, which argue it amounts to religious and ethnic profiling.

The Hindu American Foundation (HAF) and the Hindu American Political Action Committee (HAPAC) condemned the campaign as discriminatory, saying it singles out Hindu donors and that some signatories were misled or pressured into signing.

Americans4Hindus (A4H) issued a detailed response raising what it called a fundamental question: "What objective criteria determine whether an American citizen is 'RSS-linked'?" The group warned that without transparent, consistently applied standards, "such labels can become dangerously expansive and risk stigmatizing ordinary Hindu Americans who are peacefully exercising their democratic rights."

"No Hindu American should have to pass an ideological loyalty test before participating in the democratic process."

— Americans4Hindus

A4H said it would invite participating elected officials to explain how they intend to define "RSS-linked" and what safeguards they would employ to prevent religious profiling.

What This Means for Indian Americans

The pledge could reshape how campaigns scrutinize donations from the Indian-American diaspora, one of the fastest-growing donor communities in U.S. politics. It also marks a significant escalation in the domestic debate over Hindutva — the Hindu nationalist ideology that the RSS promotes — and its influence on American political funding.

Americans4Hindus urged Hindu Americans to respond with "greater civic participation" rather than withdrawal, encouraging voter registration, town hall attendance, and running for office.

For many Indian Americans, the controversy raises uncomfortable questions about where religious identity, political association, and campaign finance intersect — questions that will likely intensify as the 2026 midterm elections approach.
image_caption: Demonstrators protest outside Madison Square Garden during RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat's rally on August 29, 2026 in New York City. Nearly 90 U.S. politicians have since pledged to reject RSS-linked campaign donations.
nri_angle: About 90 US politicians pledged to reject RSS-linked campaign donations, sparking a fierce debate among Indian Americans over religious profiling and political participation ahead of the 2026 midterms.
author: Diaspora Desk
